pass_a_gloss: [Completing the previous section: the being saved signifying their having been shown] better than sin itself, and to have run beyond the nooses (βρόχος) of death. [Lemma] For I handed over to you among the first things what I also received. He says that he has handed over to them not what came into the mind simply and was received untested (ἀβασανίστως), but a gospel which he received, the one who became man for us putting into (ἐνίημι) him the knowledge; for the same [apostle] said again about the gospel, 'For neither did I receive it from a man, nor was I taught, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.' If then the one handing over is God-taught (θεοδίδακτος), how is what is proclaimed through him not true, that Christ died on behalf of our sins according to the Scriptures, clearly both the old and the new? For very many are the witnesses of the death of Christ and of the resurrection; so that it is in no way any longer doubtful (ἐνδοίαστος) that Christ Jesus died on behalf of us according to flesh, so that he might take out the sin of the world, and that he was raised again, trampling (πατέω) death, so that we too might gain (κερδαίνω) the thing. And necessarily for the present he says not only that he died but also that he was buried; for confirming (πιστόω) that he died in truth, Emmanuel was placed in a tomb; but he lived again, as I said just now; through dying in flesh giving full assurance (πληροφορέω) that he became flesh, although being God the Word; and through trampling death, showing clearly that he is God by nature. But the Word from God the Father does not make alive a foreign (ἀλλότριος) temple, nor that of someone simply, but rather his own body, through which also he is said to have died on behalf of us, so that the good of the resurrection too might be found truly to have come about on behalf of us; for the whole nature of man was in him trampling death; for so we are said to have been buried together and raised together with him, and to have sat together 'in the heavenly places.' Therefore he says that he was raised according to the Scriptures, and was seen by the holy apostles, by turns (ἀνὰ μέρος) by some as chosen, and indeed also by a multitude; and he was seen also by me as it were by the miscarried one (ἔκτρωμα) of the apostles. And he is very moderate (μετριάζω), and insists (ἰσχυρίζομαι) that he persecuted the church, but that he was shown mercy by Christ and called to apostleship; and [he] shows the great mystery of the resurrection to have been unknown neither to the ancient saints, for it had been foretold (προλέγω), nor indeed to those chosen for apostleship, who also 'became eyewitnesses (αὐτόπτης) and servants of the word.' [Lemma] But if Christ is proclaimed that he has been raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? He is struck with amazement (καταπλήσσομαι) at those who, I do not know how, have been persuaded to bear against the holy and divine Scriptures, and dare to think something other besides this. For if Christ died not so that he might remain dead, but so that, found stronger than death and corruption, he might become as it were a way and a door for the nature of man toward being able to overcome (καταθλέω) corruption and to run back (παλινδρομέω) toward life, how, he who for us [was] among the dead having been raised so that we too [might rise] with him toward life, do they still bind down (καταδεσμέω) with the nooses of death those on whose account Emmanuel, being God by nature, is said to have died and lived again? Why do they take away from the human race the goods from the resurrection, and slander (συκοφαντέω) the end (πέρας) of the dispensation with flesh? For if Christ has become firstfruits of those fallen asleep and firstborn from the dead, what is left will surely follow its own firstfruits, and would accompany (συμπαρομαρτέω) the firstborn, and very fittingly, such as a firstborn would be understood to be. And the divine Paul himself will bear witness saying, 'For if' [the quotation continues in the next section].
pass_b_english: …superior to sin itself, and to have run beyond the snares of death. “For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received” (1 Corinthians 15:3).

He says that he delivered to them, not something that had simply come into his mind and been accepted without testing, but the gospel that he received, since the one who became man for our sake put the knowledge of it into him. For the same apostle says again of the gospel, “For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1:12). If, then, the one who hands it on is taught by God, how can what he preaches not be true: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3), that is, both the Old and the New?

For the witnesses of Christ’s death and resurrection are very many, so that it can no longer be doubted in any way that Christ Jesus died for us according to the flesh, to take away the sin of the world (John 1:29), and that he rose again, trampling on death, so that we too might gain this. Here he necessarily says not only that he died but also that he was buried (1 Corinthians 15:4). For Emmanuel was laid in a tomb to confirm that he had truly died; yet he came back to life, as I said just now. By dying in the flesh he gave full assurance that the Word, though he is God, had become flesh (John 1:14); and by trampling on death he showed plainly that he is God by nature.

Yet the Word who is from God the Father does not give life to a temple foreign to him, nor simply to that of someone else, but rather to his own body, through which he is also said to have died for us, so that the good of the resurrection too might be found to have truly come about for us. For the whole of human nature was in him, trampling on death; this is how we are said to have been buried with him and raised with him (Colossians 2:12), and seated with him “in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6).

So he says that he was raised in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:4), and that he appeared to the holy apostles, to some of them separately, as chosen ones, and also to a great number at once (1 Corinthians 15:5–7). “And he appeared also to me,” as to the one untimely born among the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:8). He speaks very humbly: he insists that he persecuted the church, but that he received mercy from Christ and was called to be an apostle (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). And he shows that the great mystery of the resurrection was not unknown either to the saints of old, for it had been foretold, or to those chosen for apostleship, who also “became eyewitnesses and ministers of the word” (Luke 1:2).

“Now if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” (1 Corinthians 15:12). He is astonished at those who, I do not know how, have been persuaded to set themselves against the holy and divine Scriptures and dare to think something other than this. For if Christ died, not to remain dead, but so that, proving stronger than death and corruption, he might become a kind of way and door for human nature (John 14:6; John 10:9), so that it could prevail over corruption and run back to life, then how, now that he who for our sake was among the dead has been raised, so that we too might rise with him to life, can they still bind in the snares of death those for whose sake Emmanuel, who is God by nature, is said to have died and come back to life?

Why do they rob the human race of the good things that come from the resurrection, and slander the goal of his saving work in the flesh? For if Christ has become “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20) and “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:18), then surely what remains will follow its own firstfruits and will go along with the firstborn, and with good reason, in keeping with what a firstborn is understood to be. And the inspired Paul himself will bear witness, saying, “For if…” (Romans 6:5).
